passage:
"Look, Kalyani, she's calling you." Vasudha, in her high chair, was curling all her fingers toward her mother.
Kalyani came over. "Yes, baby?"
Vasudha looked down at the bowl of bitter gourd and pushed her flat hand out at it, hard.
"Is she waving bye to me now?" asked Grandpa.
"No, look where she's looking. That hand is for the karela."
Kalyani moved the bowl away. Vasudha curled her fingers again, at the bread basket.

qa.q: What was in the bowl Vasudha pushed her hand at?
qa.a: Bitter gourd, called karela.

qa.q: What did Vasudha's two hand gestures show she wanted?
qa.a: The curled fingers showed she wanted her mother close, and later the bread; the pushing hand showed dislike of the bitter gourd and a wish to send it away.

qa.q: How did Kalyani work out what the pushing hand meant?
qa.a: She looked at where Vasudha was looking, at the bowl, instead of guessing from the gesture alone.

qa.q: How does Grandpa read the pushing hand at first?
qa.a: Grandpa thinks it might be a wave goodbye to Kalyani, not noticing it was aimed at the food.

grounding: A toddler beckons her mother and pushes her hand out at food she dislikes, the meaning shown by where she looks.

passage: Daycare note, Thursday. At circle time, when another child brought the drum right up to Raghav's face, he pushed his hand out flat toward it and turned his head away. I moved the drum back and he settled. Later in the block corner he caught my eye and curled his fingers at me, over and over, until I came. He wanted me to see his tower. The same small hands meant "go away" and "come here" within an hour. Sunaina, daycare teacher

qa.q: What did Raghav want Sunaina to see?
qa.a: His tower in the block corner.

qa.q: What was Raghav feeling when he pushed his hand out at the drum?
qa.a: He likely felt overwhelmed or annoyed by the drum so close to his face and wanted it away; later his beckoning showed pride and a wish to share his tower.

qa.q: Which choice of Sunaina's worked, and why?
qa.a: Moving the drum back worked, because it respected his "go away" gesture and he settled quickly.

qa.q: How might the child with the drum see Raghav's pushing hand?
qa.a: The child might feel rejected or confused, having meant to share the drum.

grounding: A teacher reads a toddler's outward push as protest and his curled fingers as invitation, depending on what he is looking at.

passage:
In the courtyard of their small-town house after the rain, Nikita squatted by a puddle and curled her fingers hard toward the verandah. "Papa! Papa!"
Anand came out. There, by the puddle, sat a fat green frog.
Anand crouched beside her. The frog hopped, landing close to her toes. Nikita jerked back and pushed both flat hands out at it. "No! No!"
Anand laughed softly and lifted her up. "Too close. Let's watch from here."

qa.q: What was sitting by the puddle?
qa.a: A fat green frog.

qa.q: What changed in Nikita's feelings between the two gestures?
qa.a: First she was excited and curious and beckoned her father to share the frog; when it hopped close, she was startled and a little scared, pushing her hands out to send it away.

qa.q: What did Anand do well when the frog hopped close?
qa.a: He lifted her away and suggested watching from a distance, respecting her "go away" push.

qa.q: How might Anand feel being called out to see the frog?
qa.a: He probably feels pleased and included that Nikita wanted to share her discovery with him.

grounding: A toddler beckons her father to see a frog and pushes her hands out when it hops close, meaning shifting with what she sees.

passage: I'm Tanvir, and I was waiting outside the colony gate when little Baljeet ran toward the road. His mother raised her palm high and said, "Stop!" in a sharp voice. He froze on the kerb. Then she crouched, her face soft again, and held out her hand. He looked at her face for a long moment, then walked back and took it. He didn't cry. I don't know if he understood the hand or just the voice.

qa.q: Where did Baljeet freeze?
qa.a: On the kerb.

qa.q: What might Baljeet have been feeling when he looked at his mother's face?
qa.a: He was likely startled by the sharp "Stop!" and unsure if she was angry; her soft face seemed to reassure him, since he walked back calmly without crying.

qa.q: What did Baljeet's mother do that helped him afterwards?
qa.a: She crouched with a soft face and held out her hand, showing him he was safe and not being scolded.

qa.q: How might Baljeet's mother have felt in that moment?
qa.a: She was probably frightened for his safety at first, then relieved when he stopped and came back.

grounding: A neighbour sees a toddler stop at his mother's raised palm and sharp voice, then read her calm face as safety.

passage:
Tuesday: near the hot stove, Imran raised his palm. "Stop, Nikita." His voice was firm. Nikita's lip shook; she seemed to think he was angry. Imran smiled and picked her up.
Friday: at the stair gate, the palm went up again with the same firm word. Nikita stopped, looked up at his face, saw it was calm, and waited.
A week later, Imran raised his palm in a stop-and-go game with a grin. Nikita froze on the spot, laughing.

qa.q: Where did Imran raise his palm on Friday?
qa.a: At the stair gate.

qa.q: How had Nikita's feelings about the raised palm changed by Friday?
qa.a: On Tuesday she seemed scared that Imran was angry; by Friday she checked his calm face and felt safe enough to simply wait.

qa.q: What did Imran do on Tuesday that helped Nikita learn?
qa.a: He smiled and picked her up after the stop, showing her the firm palm meant safety, not being cross.

qa.q: What would change if Imran had used an angry face every time?
qa.a: Nikita might have learned to fear the palm and cry, instead of pausing and checking his face.

grounding: Over several days a toddler learns that her father's raised palm and firm voice mean pause, and his calm face means safety.

passage:
At the Bengaluru park, Lokesh ran full speed toward the edge of the lotus pond. His uncle Harsha lifted a palm high. "Stop, Lokesh!"
Lokesh skidded to a halt and turned. His face was ready to crumple. But Harsha's face stayed easy, and he walked up and crouched. "Water is deep. Let's look from here." Lokesh studied him, then took his hand and pointed at a lotus.

qa.q: What did Lokesh point at after taking Harsha's hand?
qa.a: A lotus.

qa.q: What was Lokesh feeling when his face was ready to crumple?
qa.a: He was probably startled and worried he was in trouble; Harsha's easy face seemed to reassure him, and he calmed enough to point at a lotus.

qa.q: What would you advise an adult who has to stop a toddler quickly?
qa.a: Use the raised palm and a firm word to stop them, then crouch with a calm face and explain, as Harsha did.

qa.q: How might Harsha have felt when Lokesh ran toward the pond?
qa.a: Harsha was likely alarmed about the deep water, yet kept a calm face so Lokesh wouldn't feel scolded.

grounding: A toddler stops at his uncle's raised palm and reads his calm face as safety rather than anger.

passage: Playgroup note, Monday. Jeevan came in bursting to tell me something with no words yet. He stretched his arms out as wide as they would go and made a rumbling noise. "A big, big truck?" qa.a: A rumbling noise.

passage:
Arnab came up from the village pond with two fish on a string. Raghav toddled ahead of him into the house, straight to Maa, and stretched his arms wide, wide, wide.
"A big fish?" Maa asked.
Raghav nodded, then pinched his fingers close together and pointed at Arnab.
"And a small one too!" Arnab laughed, holding up the tiny one. Raghav bounced, arms wide again, looking from Maa to his brother.

qa.q: How many fish did Arnab bring up from the pond?
qa.a: Two fish on a string.

qa.q: What was Raghav feeling as he stretched his arms wide for Maa?
qa.a: He was excited and proud to share the news of the big fish, bouncing and looking from Maa to his brother.

qa.q: How did Maa and Arnab help Raghav's language here?
qa.a: They put words to his gestures, "a big fish" and "a small one too", matching his wide arms and pinched fingers.

qa.q: How might Arnab feel seeing Raghav tell the story?
qa.a: Arnab likely feels amused and proud that his little brother is so excited about his catch.

grounding: A toddler uses wide arms and pinched fingers to show big and little, and his family names the meaning aloud.

passage:
At the drinking fountain in a Montreal park, Nour strained up on her toes, one arm reaching, fingers opening and closing. Jin, her neighbour, was walking her home.
"You want water?" Jin asked. Nour nodded and cupped both hands together under the spout.
Jin pressed the button. Water filled her tiny cupped hands and spilled everywhere. Nour squealed and cupped them again, looking up proudly.

qa.q: Where were Nour and Jin?
qa.a: At the drinking fountain in a Montreal park.

qa.q: What did Nour's proud look up at Jin show?
qa.a: She felt proud and delighted at catching water in her own cupped hands, and wanted Jin to see.

qa.q: What did Jin do that helped Nour?
qa.a: Jin named what her reaching meant, "You want water?", and helped her get it.

qa.q: How might it feel for Jin when Nour squeals?
qa.a: It likely feels fun and warm to see her so pleased with her small success. 😊

grounding: A toddler reaches for a fountain and cups her hands, and an adult names her want aloud.

passage: Daycare note, Wednesday. Tenzin pointed up toward the shelf and said, "Da!" I handed him the ball. He shook his head and kept pointing. I tried the blocks. Another shake. Then I followed his eyes instead of his finger. He was looking past the shelf, at a small bird on the window ledge. "Bird!" I said. He smiled wide and pointed again. Next time I will check where he is looking first. Ganga, daycare teacher

qa.q: What was Tenzin actually looking at?
qa.a: A small bird on the window ledge, past the shelf.

qa.q: What was Tenzin likely feeling when he kept pointing after getting the ball?
qa.a: He was probably frustrated at not being understood, and delighted once Ganga named the bird, as his wide smile shows.

qa.q: What did Ganga learn to do next time?
qa.a: To follow Tenzin's eyes and check what he is looking at before guessing what his pointing means.

qa.q: What was it like for Tenzin when Ganga kept handing him the wrong things?
qa.a: It was likely confusing and a little frustrating, since he wanted to share the bird, not get a toy.

grounding: A teacher learns to check what a toddler is actually looking at before guessing what his pointing means.

passage:
In the village lane in Goa, Farhan from next door crouched beside Elizabeth and pointed. "Look, a goat!" Elizabeth followed his finger and stared at the goat chewing a leaf.
Later, under the mango tree, she pointed up and grunted. Farhan reached for a low mango. "This one?"
She shook her head, still pointing. Farhan looked where her eyes were. A squirrel was running along the branch. "Oh! Squirrel!" Elizabeth grinned and bounced.

qa.q: What was the goat doing?
qa.a: Chewing a leaf.

qa.q: Why did Elizabeth shake her head when Farhan reached for the mango?
qa.a: She felt misunderstood, because she wasn't asking for the mango; she wanted to share the squirrel, and she was delighted once he saw it.

qa.q: What could Farhan do first next time Elizabeth points?
qa.a: Check where her eyes are looking before guessing, since a point can mean "look at this" as well as "I want that".

qa.a: He likely feels pleased and a bit amused that he finally found what she meant.

grounding: A toddler follows a neighbour's point and then points to share interest, and he learns to check what she is looking at.

passage:
Outside a bakery in Kyoto, Kaito pulled on Lucia's hand and pointed hard at the window. "Ah! Ah!"
"You want bread? We have bread at home," said Lucia.
Kaito pointed harder, stamping. Lucia bent down to his level and looked along his arm. Behind the bread, a grey cat lay curled on a chair. "A cat! Sleeping!" Kaito's stamping stopped. He pressed his nose to the glass, smiling.

qa.q: Where was the cat lying?
qa.a: Curled on a chair behind the bread.

qa.q: What was Kaito feeling when he pointed harder and stamped?
qa.a: He was frustrated that Lucia guessed he wanted bread; once she saw the cat, he felt understood and happy.

qa.q: What went wrong at first, and what fixed it?
qa.a: Lucia guessed the point meant "I want that"; bending down to look along his arm showed he meant "look at this", and fixed it.

qa.q: How might Lucia see the moment afterwards?
qa.a: She may feel a little sheepish about guessing bread, and glad she took a closer look.

grounding: A carer checks what a toddler is actually looking at and learns his point meant "look" rather than "I want".

passage: I'm Nilesh. I run the corner shop, and I saw it all on Saturday evening. Little Vikas wanted a lollipop, and his mother said no. His whole body went stiff as a plank. Then, just as suddenly, he flopped onto my floor, limp, and wailed. His mother didn't shout. She sat on the step beside him and waited. After a while he crawled into her lap and leaned there, heavy. It was late. Maybe he was more tired than angry.

qa.q: What did Vikas want?
qa.a: A lollipop.

qa.q: What might Vikas's stiff body and then limp flop have meant?
qa.a: The stiffness likely came from anger at hearing no, and the limp flop from being overwhelmed and tired; leaning into his mother later suggests he needed comfort and rest.

qa.q: Which choice of the mother's worked, and why?
qa.a: Staying calm and sitting nearby worked, because it gave Vikas time to settle and come to her for comfort.

qa.q: How does Nilesh see the scene?
qa.a: Nilesh watches kindly and wonders if tiredness, not just anger, was behind it, since it was late.

grounding: A shopkeeper sees a toddler stiffen and then go limp in a tantrum, and his mother calmly reads it as a need for rest and comfort.

passage:
It was late afternoon in the Mumbai flat when Usha came back from a long morning at the clinic. She walked straight to Maria, her nanny, and leaned her whole body against Maria's legs, face pressed to her knee, arms hanging loose.
"Stand up properly, Usha," her mother said. "Don't be lazy."
"She's just done in," Maria said, lifting her. Usha's head dropped onto her shoulder, and within minutes she was asleep.

passage:
The paint pot tipped over, and red spread across the kitchen floor in Haifa. Noa stood over it, tall and stiff, hands on hips. "Yara!"
Yara shrank back against the cupboard, shoulders up, eyes on her mother's body, not her face.
Noa noticed. She let out a breath, crouched down low and opened her arms. "It's okay. Come." Yara hesitated, then stepped into the hug, red footprints and all.

qa.q: What colour was the paint that spilled?
qa.a: Red.

qa.q: What was Yara feeling when she shrank back against the cupboard?
qa.a: She was frightened by her mother's tall, stiff stance, reading it as a threat before understanding any words.

qa.q: What did Noa change, and why did it help?
qa.a: She crouched low and opened her arms, a safe, open posture that told Yara she was not in danger.

qa.q: How might Noa feel after seeing Yara shrink back?
qa.a: She might feel a pang of regret, realising her stance scared Yara more than the words did.

grounding: A toddler shrinks from her mother's stiff, looming stance and comes to her when she crouches with open arms.

passage: I'm Hafsa, and I took my little brother Bhupen for his check-up. When the doctor stood right over him, tall in a white coat, Bhupen pressed his face into my side and wouldn't look. Then the nurse came and knelt on the floor, hands open, smiling. Bhupen peeked. He stared at her a long time. Then he held out his arm for her to look at. I can't say what changed for him. Maybe it was just her kneeling.

qa.q: What did the nurse do when she came in?
qa.a: She knelt on the floor with her hands open, smiling.

qa.q: What might Bhupen have been feeling when the doctor stood over him?
qa.a: He was likely scared of the tall figure looming over him; the nurse kneeling seems to have made him feel safer and more curious.

qa.q: What could the doctor learn from the nurse?
qa.a: Getting down to a child's level with an open posture can help a small child feel safe enough to cooperate.

qa.q: How does Hafsa experience the check-up?
qa.a: Hafsa feels her brother pressed against her side and is unsure what changed, noticing it might have been the kneeling.

grounding: A sister sees her toddler brother hide from a standing doctor and relax toward a kneeling nurse.

passage:
"Jahnavi, go to Chetan chacha! He came all the way from Dubai."
Jahnavi buried her face in her mother's neck and clung tight.
"She's being rude," said Dadi.
"She's scared, Mummy-ji. She's never seen him. And that beard!"
Chetan laughed and sat down on the floor, far off. "No hurry." He started building a tower of cups.
After a while, Jahnavi turned her head and peeked at the tower.

qa.q: What did Chetan start building?
qa.a: A tower of cups.

qa.q: What was Jahnavi feeling when she buried her face in her mother's neck?
qa.a: She felt shy and afraid of a stranger she had never seen, not rude.

qa.q: Which of Chetan's choices worked, and why?
qa.a: Sitting on the floor far off and playing with cups worked, because Jahnavi could watch him and warm up without pressure.

qa.q: How does Dadi see Jahnavi's clinging?
qa.a: Dadi sees it as rudeness to a guest, rather than fear of someone new.

grounding: A toddler hides her face and clings when meeting a new uncle, and he lets her warm up at her own pace.

passage:
In a busy café in Valencia, a waiter dropped a tray of plates behind them. Crash! Clara's whole body jerked, arms flung out wide, and then she froze, eyes huge. A second later she began to wail.
"Such a fuss," a man at the next table muttered.
Yara scooped her up and held her close, rocking. "Big bang. You're safe. I've got you," she said softly, again and again, until Clara's arms went soft around her neck.

qa.q: What did the waiter drop?
qa.a: A tray of plates.

qa.q: What was Clara feeling when her arms flung out and she froze?
qa.a: She was startled and frightened by the sudden crash; her wail shows her body was still shaken.

qa.q: What did Yara do that helped Clara's body settle?
qa.a: She held her close, rocked her and repeated soft, calm words until Clara relaxed.

qa.q: How does the man at the next table see Clara's reaction?
qa.a: He sees it as a fuss, not as a small child's automatic fright at a loud noise.

grounding: A toddler flinches and freezes at a sudden crash, a reflex, and her mother's soothing voice and hold settle her.

passage: I'm Nazia, Ira's cousin. On Sunday I was in the kitchen when the pressure cooker let out its loud whistle. Ira, on the floor with her doll, jumped so hard she fell sideways, arms out. Then she went completely still. Her aunt laughed, "Scaredy!" Ira's mother picked her up and said, "Loud, na? I've got you." Ira held on tight. I don't know if she was scared or just surprised, but her little heart was going fast.

qa.q: What made the loud whistle?
qa.a: The pressure cooker.

qa.q: What might Ira have been feeling when she went completely still?
qa.a: She was startled and probably frightened by the sudden whistle; holding on tight shows she needed comfort to settle.

qa.q: What would you tell the aunt who laughed?
qa.a: That Ira's jump was an automatic reaction, not silliness, and that a calm word and a hold help more than teasing.

qa.q: How might Ira's mother see the moment?
qa.a: She sees a child who needs comforting, so she picks her up and speaks softly.

grounding: A cousin sees a toddler flinch and freeze at a loud whistle, and her mother soothes her rather than teasing.

passage:
Monday: the wind slammed the balcony door. Shreya flinched hard, arms flying out, and screamed. Rashmi held her close and hummed until she stopped shaking.
Thursday: before switching on the mixer, Rashmi picked her up. "Loud noise coming." Shreya still froze at the roar, but only for a moment.
The following Tuesday: the mixer started. Shreya jumped a little, looked at Rashmi's face, and went back to her blocks.

qa.q: What slammed on Monday?
qa.a: The balcony door, slammed by the wind.

qa.q: What was Shreya feeling on Monday when she flinched and screamed?
qa.a: She was startled and frightened by the sudden bang; her body needed comfort to stop shaking.

qa.q: Which habit of Rashmi's helped over the week?
qa.a: Warning her before loud noises and holding her, so Shreya's body could settle faster each time.

qa.q: How might Rashmi feel when Shreya goes back to her blocks?
qa.a: She would likely feel relieved and pleased that Shreya now settles quickly.

grounding: Over a week a mother helps her toddler settle after startle reflexes with a warning, a soothing voice and a hold.
